column4: Laurie Anderson: The Chalkroom, Citizens, Ocean / Canoe and paintings
column8: The Chalkroom (with Hsin-Chien Huang), a room of white words on black lit by black light; Citizens (2021), a video of 19 people sharpening knives; Ocean / Canoe (2026), a gold canoe broken and repaired; and five large paintings first shown at the Hirshhorn in 2021.

column4: Into the Light: Perfectly Clear, Hind Sight and more
column8: A survey of Turrell's light works over several decades, using light as a sculptural material that changes how you see space. Perfectly Clear (a Ganzfeld) and Hind Sight need a timed reservation.
A Skyspace 40 feet across, built inside a former concrete water tank: an opening in the roof frames the sky. Dawn and dusk light programs need a reservation.

column4: Étroits sont les Vaisseaux (Narrow Are the Vessels), The Women of the Revolution, Velimir Chlebnikov
column8: Large sculptures and paintings shown with the Hall Art Foundation: a wave of cast concrete with rebar and lead (2002), lead beds with photographs (1992) and a cycle of paintings (2004). Seasonal: open May to October.
Hundreds of handmade instruments, among them a 9-foot banjo and an 8-foot marimba, built by the Bennington College teacher; visitors may play them.
150 light fixtures with 417 bulbs hang in a curve like the Milky Way; their creamy glow is the average color of the universe.
A 10 × 20 foot mural of hand-glazed tiles that leads visitors into the galleries, mixing painting and architecture.
Two motorized glass and metal units turn 45 degrees between the old columns, redirecting views toward the north windows and the Hoosic River; visitors push them to move them.
A 9 × 16 foot watercolor of the second floor of Building 6 before its renovation: about an acre with some 400 columns.

column4: Hello America: 40 Hits from the 50 States
column8: A wall painting layering Berkshire tree silhouettes, a dusky landscape, big camouflaged slogans and forty quotations from American sources, after J.G. Ballard's novel Hello America.

column4: Photographs of the Sprague Electric factory
column8: Photographs Whitman began in 1988 of the abandoned Sprague Electric factory, the mill buildings that are now MASS MoCA, and traces of the people who worked there.

column3: Morehshin Allahyari, Lauren Lee McCarthy, Analia Saban and others
column8: A group show about how people relate to each other, to their devices and to the future as technology changes daily life. Lauren Lee McCarthy's LAUREN: Anyone Home? runs daily 12–3 pm. On view through July 25, 2027.
Photographs, collages and new installations about how race, money and empire shape daily life and resistance, curated by Terence Washington. On view through November 22, 2026.

Everyday things (shoes, pails, cardboard, glass) paired and lit so that the gallery's hidden parts, like vents and outlets, stand out; it also nods to the self-service car wash next door. On view through February 21, 2027.

A tilted floor of handmade fresco tiles that works as an instrument: contact microphones amplify your footsteps as you cross it. Rivera mixes ancient fresco methods with sound to think about how cultures and colonial histories travel. On view through June 13, 2027.

Film, sound and sculpture: household-sized speculative tools cast shadows across a 100-foot film about Sarno's weaving studies in Peru and Argentina, made with collaborators mostly from the Global South. On view through January 31, 2027.

column3: Cecilia Vicuña, Sam Frésquez, Lola Ayisha Ogbara
column8: A three-part show that starts from Cecilia Vicuña's precarios, with her Quipu Desaparecido 2 (2018) and Balsa Snake Raft to Escape the Flood (2017), about impermanence, remembrance and cycles. On view through April 4, 2027.

column3: Roberta Bayley, R. Crumb, Shepard Fairey, Bob Gruen, Chris Stein and others
column8: Eleven silk screens by Gary Lichtenstein Editions that reimagine images from PUNK Magazine, in the R&D Store's gallery. On view through January 3, 2027.
A 100-foot work of painted and cut-out flowers, grown or gathered by the artist, that follows a New England growing season from late April to mid-September. In the Hunter hallway.
The stairwell and basement of Building 10 turned into a musical instrument played by the building's sounds and by visitors; a knob and dial change the mood from ambient to party.
Eleven concrete structures designed with Shohei Shigematsu (OMA), outdoors on the campus, where visitors are invited to make their own sounds, gather, perform or watch the stars.
Four pink totems about 25 feet tall in metal, epoxy and concrete, on loan from the Hall Art Foundation; first shown in Paris in 2007 and here for their US debut.
Two red oak saplings, one from the Southeast and one from the Northeast, grow side by side in planters, a plant-relocation project about climate change, with bleachers for cheering them on.

column4: all utopias fell (The Shining and The Library of the Sun)
column8: A retro satellite made from an Airstream trailer seems to have crash-landed above the Boiler House, with parachutes and solar panels; inside, The Library of the Sun mixes home, lab and library. Seasonal: open May to October.
A sound installation in the old heating plant mixing ambient recordings with parts of a Paul Park story; it grows louder or softer as you move. Seasonal: open May to October.

A big painting in house paint over the four walls of the bike tunnel under Building 6, based on the placeholder text designers use, with mirrors set among the painted parts. Seasonal: open May to October.

A 40-foot sculpture of laminated timber and plywood wrapped in chain-link fence, with a gold-leaf shackle near the top; first made for Madison Square Park in New York. At the southern edge of the campus, toward Main Street.
The bells of the old factory clock tower played by a program that follows the sunlight: the tones change with the weather and the time of day, stop at dusk, and the clock faces glow at night.
A 20-channel sound piece in the walkway between the lobby and the Sol LeWitt building: the held notes of 24 singers aged 7 to 75 move along the walkway as you walk.
A granite boulder sawn in half hangs about 10 feet up, the halves 11 inches apart, held by steel supports and cables. Near the entry walkway and the Clocktower.

One hundred coins, each with a small drawing of a coin in a corner, hidden in corners all over the museum, from galleries to the café and restrooms ("coin" is French for corner). A scavenger hunt through the buildings.

Short texts by the author and historian Joe Manning beside the mill windows, about the trains, hills, rivers and buildings of North Adams you can see through them, drawn from his books and residents' memories. Windows throughout the museum.
A short-term exhibition by the Miami artist Jillian Mayer, listed on the museum's October 2026 map in Building 6, second floor.

Grasso's films (OttO, Anima, Orchid Island, Geophonia, Cosmic Drive) with new paintings, steel Cosmic Mirrors and a white-bronze Future Herbarium, shown without labels inside three X-shaped structures that steer how you look through the huge gallery. Opens November 7, 2026.
